transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 09:30 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood), Ethan Park (Redwood), Liam O'Neil (Redwood - recruiter), Brianna Cho (candidate, QuantFlow Labs)

Summary:
Quick culture/technical screen for senior inference engineer role. Focused on Brianna's recent experience with model quantization, NVLink infra, latency debugging, and tradeoffs for private deployments. Agreed next step: short take-home design prompt and potential on-site panel.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Liam: All right joining now, hey Brianna, thank you for making time, I'm Liam from talent, quick mic check?
[00:00:08] Brianna: Yep, hi hi, can you hear me?
[00:00:10] Maya: Loud and clear. This is Maya Chen, hiring manager for inference systems. Ethan's on for a technical peek. We'll run ~30-45 minutes, some culture, some tech, then next steps.
[00:00:24] Ethan: Morning! quick note I might jump in with some deep-dive questions around batching and KV cache, hope that's ok?
[00:00:30] Brianna: Yeah totally, happy to.
[00:00:35] Maya: Cool. So to start, can you give a quick 5-minute walk through of what you've been shipping at QuantFlow the last year, high level and then one or two problems you personally owned.
[00:00:48] Brianna: Sure. So last year I led the inference stack for our real-time scoring product. It's a multi-tenant service that serves dozens of models, mostly transformer encoders and some encoder-decoder for summarization. I owned the runtime optimizations - so kernel selection, custom batching, and work on int8 quant pipelines. One concrete thing - we had a tail latency issue when sequence length spiked, turned out to be a bad padding strategy plus nvlink saturation when large KV caches were being materialized across shards. I prototyped a prefix-aware batcher and moved some KV materialization to a pinned worker, which reduced p95 by about 40 percent.
[00:01:34] Ethan: Quick clarify - when you say "KV materialization" you mean populating the key-value cache across model partitions?
[00:01:39] Brianna: Yeah exactly, across two-GPU partitioning. We had a sharded KV store that on cold starts would stream segments over PCIe and NVLink, and we were paying a lot in inter-GPU transfer.
[00:01:51] Maya: Nice. Any particular tooling you used to profile that? like nsight, perf, or internal tracing?
[00:01:58] Brianna: We leaned on NVIDIA Nsight and some homegrown tracing that tags token latencies. Also used eBPF for kernel queue depth shadows — not perfect but helped correlate syscalls with the timeline. Some traces were noisy, transcription here please — I mean some traces were noisy but helped.
[00:02:16] [interruption - brief static]
[00:02:20] Liam: minor echo on my end but yeah we're good.
[00:02:24] Ethan: Got it. How comfortable are you with quantization pipelines in prod? like int8 calibration, per-channel scales, dynamic vs static quant?
[00:02:33] Brianna: Pretty comfortable. I shipped quantized models using post-training static quant with per-channel granularity for weights and per-tensor for activations. For us, dynamic quant caused hallucinations on certain token distributions, so we added a calibration dataset derived from real query traffic and kept some model heads in full-precision for sensitive outputs. We also wrote unit tests to check perplexity drift on key prompts.
[00:02:58] Maya: Interesting tradeoff, did you measure delta in quality vs cost? numbers?
[00:03:04] Brianna: On our main N=2048 transformer compressing to int8 we saw token throughput improve ~2.3x and cost per token down about 45 percent but BLEU/perplexity drift was small for most inputs, except for long-form summarization where F1 dropped 6-8 percent on edge cases. So we gated that pipeline with a policy router.
[00:03:24] Ethan: When you mention policy router is that an application layer that picks FP vs int8 model based on request features?
[00:03:30] Brianna: Yeah, basically request heuristics + a small learned classifier we trained to detect sensitive prompts. It adds a tiny bit of latency but avoids quality regressions.
[00:03:38] [00:03:40] Ethan: Nice. Walk me through a time you debugged a perf regression in production that wasn't obvious.
[00:03:45] Brianna: One time we saw a 30% increase in p95 across a cluster after a model rollout. We rolled back eventually but root cause was a change in tokenization that increased average sequence length; combined with the new model's KV access pattern, it pushed the batching window into a different regime, increasing the serialization overhead. It took us a bit to instrument the batching scheduler to log sequence histograms. We then adjusted batching policy: max batch bytes and prioritized short queries, which flattened the tail.
[00:04:20] Maya: Do you have experience with model rollouts A/B or canary for large models?
[00:04:25] Brianna: Yes. We did canary rollouts with traffic mirroring and shadow testing. Canary had 1-2% traffic, we monitored latency, perplexity on holdout prompts, and rollback if any metric tripped. Also did multi-variant rollouts for quantized vs fp32.
[00:04:40] Ethan: Nice. How do you think about autoscaling for steady vs spiky workloads?
[00:04:46] Brianna: For steady state, we scale by utilization and queue length with predictive warmers for known daily patterns. For spikes, we prefer horizontal autoscaling with pre-warmed pools because cold-start of a model on a GPU is costly. We also experimented with hybrid strategies — dedicated warm nodes for tail traffic, while best-effort requests go to burst pool.
[00:05:05] [00:05:10] Maya: Ok switching gears a bit: culture/teaming. What's your preferred level of ownership? Do you like deep individual contributor work or more cross-team orchestration?
[00:05:20] Brianna: I like a mix. I enjoy digging into kernels and perf, but I also like owning a surface area and coordinating with infra and SRE folks. At QuantFlow I paired closely with SRE to automate rollout playbooks. I also mentored two junior engineers on inference primitives.
[00:05:39] Liam: quick recruiter check — what's your availability for a 2-hour onsite panel if we move forward?
[00:05:45] Brianna: I could do late September, earliest 9/28, otherwise early October.
[00:05:50] Liam: Noted.
[00:05:53] Ethan: Technical follow-up: have you worked with private deployments or VPC connectors for customer data isolation?
[00:05:59] Brianna: Yes, QuantFlow offered a VPC-hosted tenant option. We had to ensure no cross-tenant mem leaks and also provide KMS integration for model keys. Biggest issue was observability — when you push logs into a customer-controlled VPC you lose a lot of central telemetry, so we built a secure metrics relay with envelope encryption.
[00:06:19] Maya: Nice. Do you have SSO/enterpise compliance exposure? SOC2, audits?
[00:06:25] Brianna: I worked on the SOC2 readiness docs, mostly around change control for model weights and access logs. I coordinated with compliance for audit traces when we deploy new model versions.
[00:06:35] [00:06:40] Ethan: Hypothetical: We're hitting a budget constraint on an enterprise customer but they need deterministic latency. What levers do you pull?
[00:06:48] Brianna: First look at model architecture choices: distillation or smaller model families; then runtime levers: batching policy, prefix caching, KV sharding, quantization. Also route by SLA: premium customers get reserved capacity while other traffic uses shared pools. Finally, consider model edits to reduce sequence length or cache-friendly prompts.
[00:07:10] Maya: Good. Any scale numbers you can share — largest cluster you worked on, GPU counts, requests per second?
[00:07:16] Brianna: Largest was ~120 GPUs across 6 NVLink pods, serving ~4k RPS at peak for small token windows, tail p95 ~220ms before optimizations.
[00:07:28] Ethan: That's helpful. A couple quick whiteboard-y questions — nothing formal — how would you design a prefix cache for multi-tenant inference? High level is fine.
[00:07:37] Brianna: High level: cache keyed by model_id + prefix_hash + tenant_policy. Keep entries sharded by GPU affinity to reduce cross-GPU pulls. Eviction policy should be LRU with hot-list promotion and size-aware TTLs. For privacy, encrypt tenant cache on disk and ensure per-tenant namespace. For multi-tenant fairness, limit cache slots per tenant with a shared pool for long tails.
[00:08:03] Ethan: Any thoughts about sharding strategy for very large KV per sequence?
[00:08:08] Brianna: Shard by attention head groups or by token range depending on access pattern; for long contexts, token-range sharding reduces RG memory blowup. Balance with NVLink hops though.
[00:08:18] [00:08:20] Maya: Interviewer note: Brianna uses precise language and has strong infra instincts.
[00:08:24] Brianna: thanks.
[00:08:26] Liam: Quick plug — any open compensation expectations so recruiting can match bands?
[00:08:30] Brianna: I'm looking for something in the low- to mid-senior band, primarily base plus equity, flexible on title.
[00:08:37] Liam: Great.
[00:08:40] Maya: Two final questions: one behavioral, one technical. Behavioral: Tell me about a time you had to influence a non-technical stakeholder on an engineering tradeoff.
[00:08:51] Brianna: We had product push for higher recall which required heavier models. I built a cost/benefit dashboard showing latency and cost impact and ran a short A/B on a subset. Framing it as customer impact (time to answer) helped product accept a hybrid plan where we used larger models for premium customers.
[00:09:10] Maya: Technical: If you had to choose between aggressive batching to reduce cost and single-request latency SLO, how do you balance?
[00:09:18] Brianna: Tradeoffs: batching reduces cost but increases queuing. I'd define SLO tiers — e.g., <100ms for interactive, allow 200-400ms for background. Use dynamic batching windows with priority preemption for interactive requests. Also use pre-warmed instances for low-latency paths and best-effort pooled GPUs for batched workloads.
[00:09:39] Ethan: Quick nit: any experience with kernel-level optimizations or writing custom CUDA kernels?
[00:09:45] Brianna: I wrote some fused kernels for attention patterns in PyTorch with Triton prototypes; not a lot of low-level C++ CUDA but enough to collaborate with the infra team.
[00:09:57] Maya: Great. That's about the time we had set. Any questions for us?
[00:10:03] Brianna: Yeah two quick ones: team makeup and how much ownership a senior engineer has over infra?
[00:10:10] Maya: We're a compact team of ~8 infra+runtime engineers, seniors typically lead a project and own rollout playbooks end-to-end including vendor interactions if needed.
[00:10:20] Ethan: And we prioritize folks who can both ship infra and mentor; lots of cross-collab with product.
[00:10:27] Brianna: Sounds good. One more: what's the typical interview timeline after a take-home?
[00:10:31] Liam: Usually 1 week to review the take-home, then on-site within 2 weeks if green.
[00:10:36] Brianna: Perfect.
[00:10:38] Maya: Great, thanks Brianna. We'll send the design prompt and rubric, and Liam will follow up on compensation and scheduling.
[00:10:46] Brianna: Thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[00:10:48] Liam: Thanks, bye.
